newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COCOA - Farmers begin to benefit from tax law.
newsitem.headline: COCOA - Farmers begin to benefit from tax law.

text.p: Bahia cocoa farmers this week began to feel the benefits of the abolition of a 13 percent sales tax on agricultural exports
The Brazilian Senate last week voted to abolish the ICMS tax, which is levied at state level, and the law came into effect this week after being sanctioned by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
"Today, the international price is roughly the same as it was last Friday before the tax was officially abolished," said one farmer.
"However, last week I was receiving 15 Real per (15 kilo) arroba and today I am getting 17.5 Real." the farmer said. "It won't save me but it will help me."

However, the National Cocoa Producers Council (CNPC) said that not all purchasers, who were responsible for paying the taxes but in practice discounted them off the amount paid to farmers, were passing on the difference.
"Some farmers are only receiving 16.5 Real. We are going to watch the situation very closely to make sure that everyone passes on the difference," said CNPC president Wallace Sententa.
Setenta said that producers were still waiting to receive government credits that have been promised for this year to help them fight witch's broom disease.

However, he said it was unlikely that they would be able to collect the money until November or December. He said that so far the two banks responsible for distributing the money had received a total of 3,572 applications for credits from farmers for an amount totalling 77.79 million Real.
"The credits farmers received last year helped alot," he said. "The problem was that it wasn't very wide-ranging. Only a few farmers benefitted."

"Last year's crop was 2.6 million (60-kilo) bags but we had good weather. This year's will come to around 2.4 million but this is because of a drought. If it had rained more, we would have had 3.1 or 3.2 million," Setenta said.
The current midcrop, or temporao, will finish at the end of September.
Arrivals for this week were a surprisingly high total of 209,329 bags, compared to 25,729 in the previous week and 43,903 the week before that.
Dealers said this was due to one major buyer of beans adjusting its figures this week.
"Somebody who hadn't been declaring their beans for several months decided to do it this week. They wanted people to think Bahia was producing less cocoa than it actually was," one dealer explained.
"There has certainly been no surge in harvesting this week."
